analysis.one_liner: Permanently bars new roads and most logging in undeveloped sections of America's national forests.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Energy Committee and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made permanent a national rule against building new roads in the roughly undeveloped "inventoried roadless" parts of the national forests, and against cutting timber there, with narrow exceptions for safety, existing leases, and habitat or fire-risk work. Supporters said this protects the drinking water for millions of Americans, wildlife habitat, and recreation areas at almost no cost to the national timber supply. The bill was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who drink water drawn from forest watersheds — the bill cites more than 354 municipal watersheds on roadless areas serving millions of citizens — plus hikers, hunters, anglers, and campers who use these public lands, and downstream communities that save on water filtration costs. Future generations inherit the watersheds, wildlife habitat, and undeveloped recreation land instead of road networks built for timber extraction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who drinks water and uses public lands

how_it_helps.text: It bars new road construction and reconstruction in inventoried roadless areas of the National Forest System, protecting more than 354 municipal watersheds that provide drinking water to millions of citizens [S3].
It protects habitat for threatened and endangered species and prevents fragmentation of the landscape by road corridors [S3].

It preserves land for hunting, fishing, camping, and other recreation, and the bill notes that keeping roadless areas undisturbed saves downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry and road contractors, who lose access to timber and road-building in roadless areas; the bill's own findings put the cost at under 0.5% of the national timber supply. Communities hoping for resource extraction jobs in those areas also lose that potential, though the bill allows many current uses to continue unchanged.

drawbacks.text: The bill locks in its prohibitions: it states they cannot be reconsidered, revised, or rescinded in future forest-plan decisions [S3], which removes flexibility for future managers and communities if circumstances change.

Logging and road-building are barred in roadless areas except through narrow exceptions, which the timber industry and some rural communities that depend on forest work have historically argued costs jobs and local revenue; the bill itself concedes it removes areas from timber supply, though it says the impact is under half a percent of national timber output [S3].

The Tongass National Forest in Alaska, the country's largest national forest, is carved out for activities already noticed before January 2001, weakening the bill's coverage where old-growth logging pressure is greatest [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — permanent protection of watersheds that supply drinking water to millions, fish and wildlife habitat, and recreation lands — are broad and lasting, while the costs are small and concentrated: the bill's own findings note that protecting roadless areas would affect less than 0.5% of the national timber supply and a fraction of the tiny share of national oil and gas that national forests produce [S3]. The main honest objection is that the bill locks in its rules and bars ordinary plan-level reconsideration, which reduces land managers' flexibility if conditions change; the bill addresses this through exception processes and a NEPA-reviewed map-modification authority, though those rely on administrative judgment rather than a public vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action until Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 17, 2011 and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5].
That referral was the last action of any kind; the committee never held a hearing or markup, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Logging, road-building, and resource-extraction interests are better off because the bill died, since the roadless areas it would have locked up remain open to future development decisions.

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give lasting protection to inventoried roadless areas of the National Forest System.

for.name: 19 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Bingaman, the Energy Committee's chairman, giving it senior support on the committee of jurisdiction.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 listed sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Lieberman, with no Republican support, and the committee referral was the end of the road.

industries.note: The bill bans cutting, selling, or removing timber in inventoried roadless areas, with exceptions only for infrequent, narrowly defined habitat and fire-risk work [S2, S3]. The bill's findings say this would affect less than 0.5% of the national timber supply [S3].

industries.industry: Road contractors and oil, gas, and mining interests
industries.note: New roads in roadless areas would be barred except for safety, emergency, existing mineral leases, and other narrow cases, limiting future access for resource development [S2, S3].
Hikers, hunters, anglers, and the businesses that serve them keep large undeveloped forests open for recreation, which the bill explicitly protects alongside its prohibitions [S3].

industries.industry: Municipal water systems and downstream communities
industries.note: Undisturbed roadless watersheds supply clean water to millions and spare communities the cost of building water filtration plants, benefits the bill documents in its findings [S3].
